Bre-X Minerals Ltd., once hailed as Canada's next big thing in gold mining, disappeared overnight in what may go down as the biggest fraud in history. In a stunning collapse that left 10,000 investors with worthless stock and shaken Canada's regulatory system to its core, Bre-X disintegrated on Tuesday after a key Indonesian gold deposit was found to contain no gold. 

Less than 24 hours earlier, Bre-X had announced an astonishing 800 million oz (24 tonnes) gold discovery at the Bulongan site on the island of Borneo. But by Tuesday, Indonesia's state mining company, which had joined Bre-X in a 50-50 venture there, said tests showed no gold was present. 

Canada's Toronto Stock Exchange, which had allowed Bre-X's smaller Pacific Richfield unit to trade without regulatory approval since last autumn, scrapped the company's stocks on Tuesday. Trading in Bre-X's main unit was suspended on Monday at the request of the company which had said it would announce a major discovery. 

In a scramble to protect their reputations and investors, Canadian regulators barred Bre-X from raising any more money. But it was too late to save millions of dollars, possibly billions, which flowed into Bre-X in recent months as it made one sensational gold discovery after another on the sparsely populated island of Borneo. 

"This is a total fraud. It's a Ponzi scheme that's collapsed," said John Dahlin, director of investigations for the Ontario Securities Commission (OSC), Canada's biggest markets regulator. 

The OSC had launched hearings on Monday to revoke Bre-X's Pacific Richfield unit's trading licence after it was discovered that the company had not filed prospectuses for those units since last October. 

"We have been warning the public not to deal in these stocks since last fall," said Dahlin, who added that the OSC had received hundreds of complaints from angry investors. 

Bre-X's dramatic fall from grace began in earnest on Friday when Indonesia's antiquated state mining company, Perusahaan Pertambangan Negara (PPN), said it had sold its half-interest in the Bulongan site to Bre-X for 1.3 billion rp (C$100 million) in cash and shares. 

PPN's sudden sale shocked Indonesian mining officials and raised suspicions that the gold deposit may not exist. 

"This is the biggest thing that's ever happened in Canada and it may be the biggest thing that's ever happened in the world," said Stephen Leeb, a New York-based investment advisor who had warned clients to sell Bre-X stocks in October.

But now those same investors are left with the biggest of all scares -- the fear that they may have been the victims of the biggest gold swindle in history. In what may go down as Canada's biggest capital scandal, Bre-X and its Indonesian subsidiary, PT Freeport Betama, have been accused of orchestrating a fabulously profitable -- but utterly bogus -- gold mine. The shock waves from this debacle are still reverberating through Canada's financial markets and regulatory agencies -- and may eventually be felt on Wall Street. "This could be the most significant case in the history of Canadian capital markets," Chris Evans, a Toronto-based spokesman for the Canadian Institute of Chartered Financial Analysts, said on Monday. But late last week, Canadian and U.S. regulators slapped trading freezes on Bre-X and PT Freeport Betama after stunned investors sold those stocks for the exits. U.S. trading was halted on Friday at the instigation of the company's U.S. lawyer, Fasken Martineau DuMoulin LLP, who also represents Bre-X's Canadian unit, the company said. Giering on Thursday denied there was any merit to the notion that his company's decision to go public was driven by a desire to escape taxes through a headquarters location in the United Mountain time zone. "I think it's ridiculous," Giering told Reuters in a telephone interview from New York, where he was holding meetings with investors and analysts. "I've never even discussed taxes with anyone in connection with coming public," he said. "It's just another one of these crazy stories that seems to come along every time we take one of these steps to remold our company for the 21st century," he added. The NCR leader was referring to the succession of transformation steps he has engineered over the last several years to reposition the former technology leader for the new realities of a post-PC era. "We've all been here for the last one of these, and we know what to do," the chairman said, referring to the damping effect such distractions have on both the stock and momentum of the Daly city, Calif. company's stock. "We'll get through this one too," he said. The leader of the old computer industry bellwether said he had met with several leading institutional investors and analysts on Thursday, and he expected to add still more to the list of more than 50 who have agreed to back the company's plans to go before the Securities and Exchange Commission in a few weeks and begin trading as a regular public company "in about six to eight weeks time," he estimated. "We're in the home stretch here," Giering said. A spokesman for the chairman said he had been scheduled to meet with AT&T Corp. officials on Friday, but he said this was just a routine planning of the leader's New Jersey schedule and one that had been in place for several days. "There's nothing new here," the spokesman said, adding that it was "just one of these New Jersey (NJ) trips he makes from time to time." The spokesman declined to comment on what business matters may have been on the leader's agenda when he met with AT&T officials on previous visits to the New Jersey headquarters of the telecom giant. "There's no AT&T connection here at all," the NCR spokesman said, adding that "it's just one of these crazy rumors that start every time we take one of these steps to remold our company for the 21st century." He said plans to move the company headquarters were still under consideration and that no decision had been reached. "We'll make this decision based on what's best for shareholders and the long-term future of the company," the spokesman said. "The leader is free to choose any headquarters location that he thinks is best," he added. With NCR's headquarters currently located in Daly City, Calif., just outside San Francisco, the company is subject to California and the highest-in-the-United-States corporate tax rates in the state of New York. A shift to New Jersey would allow the company to enjoy the lower taxes of that state and place it in the same mountain time zone as AT&T, which some believe could help the company align more closely with the telecom giant's business cycles. While Giering downplayed the importance of taxes as a factor in the company's decision to go public, he acknowledged that a headquarters relocation could help improve the company's cost structure. response: VLSI Technology Inc expects flat to lower revenues for the 1997 first quarter compared to the 1996 fourth quarter's net revenues of $183.6 million, a spokesman for the company said. Allen Marcow, VLSI's vice president of corporate communications, confirmed that company executives had warned analysts in a conference call about the outlook on revenues. "We did not see a lot of Q1 growth in revenues," Marcow told Reuters, referring to comments made to analysts. Marcow also said VLSI expects to see continued improvements from expense controls. He said gross profit margins would improve in 1997 due to a changing product mix. Analysts said the Friday afternoon conference call heightened concern about VLSI's fourth quarter results. Even before the call, worry about the data had caused the stock to fall sharply throughout the day. VLSI shares were down 6-3/8 to 16-7/8 at 1453 EST/1953 GMT. The stock was the most active Nasdaq issue, with nearly 15 millions shares changing hands. The sell-off began slowly this morning, then picked up steam ahead of the conference call, which began at 1300 EST/1800 GMT. The sharp decline in VLSI's stock followed the release of the company's results for the 1996 fourth quarter. The release came after the stock market close Thursday. The company reported a loss of $1.38 a share after a pre-announced charge for closing a factory. On an operating basis, earnings of $0.17 a share were in line with the First Call consensus. But market sources said the report fell short of Wall Street's informal, "whispered" expectations for the fourth quarter, traditionally a strong one for the company. Merrill Lynch analyst Tom Kurlak, who listened in on the conference call, said he expected analysts' consensus estimate on VLSI earnings for fiscal 1997 to fall in the coming days to around $1.20 per share. Kurlak said two main negatives drove the stock down Friday: projected flatness in first quarter revenues, and a delayed reaction to the Wednesday resignation of VLSI Chief Financial Officer Gregrory Hinckley. Hinckley left to join Mentor Graphics Corp as finance chief and chief operating officer. He was replaced at VSLI by Bala Iyer, the company's former controller. Kurlak also said product orders for the company had declined in the fourth quarter. "We are not setting up for momentum in the first half," he said, referring to the company's sales momentum heading into 1997. On a more upbeat note, Kurlak said he expected the company to see gross margins rise slightly in the first quarter to around 42.2 percent from 41.5 percent in the fourth quarter. As a result, the analyst said he still forecasts that earnings will grow sequentially in the first quarter to $0.20 a share, compared to operating earnings of $0.17 reported for the forth quarter.

response: The stock of VLSI Technology Inc. took a nose-dive Friday, losing over 25 percent of its value, after projecting that revenues in the 1997 first quarter would be equal to or below the fourth quarter of 1996. VLSI stock fell $5.875 to close at $17.325 on Nasdaq Friday. More than 19 million shares changed hands, topping the Nasdaq actives list. The San Jose, Calif.-based high technology company late Thursday reported a loss for the fourth quarter of 1996 of $63.6 million, or $1.38 a share, on revenues of $183.6 million, including a pre-announced charge for closing a factory. After speaking with analysts, VLSI's vice president of corporate communications Allen Marcow said, "We did not see a lot of first quarter growth in revenues" compared with revenues the 1996 fourth quarter. In the 1996 first quarter, the quarter that will be used for comparison when 1997 figures are released, VLSI earned $3.2 million, or 7 cents a share, on revenues of $167.7 million. VLSI appears to be facing competition or other problems in three of its four business groups, said C.B. Lee, an analyst at Hancock Institutional Equity Services. Problem areas are computing, hurt by the recent sales slowdown at a key customer Apple Computer Inc.; digital entertainment where it faces stiff competition from SGS-Thomson, and the Compass software unit. The key exception is VLSI's wireless communications chip business, which remains strong, Lee said. Merrill Lynch analyst Tom Kurlak said the stock decline was also a delayed reaction to the Wednesday resignation of VLSI Chief Financial Officer Gregrory Hinckley. Hinckley left to join Mentor Graphics Corp. as finance chief and chief operating officer. He was replaced at VSLI by Bala Iyer, the company's former controller. The San Jose, Calif.-based company is a maker of high-end Application Specific Integrated Circuits (ASICs) used in communications, digital entertainment and, to a declining extent, in personal computers. For several years, the company has been undergoing a transition out of the computer chipset business and into more profitable areas such as communications and TV set-top boxes.

response: (Corrects by deleting the fourth paragraph, so that the story will reflect that at no point did Giering blame AT&T for tax issues that NCR faces as an independent company.) NCR Corp eked out a small profit in the fourth quarter of 1996 and saw healthy gains in year-over-year profit margins but hopes of matching computer industry growth rates remain a long way off, executives said. In a conference call with analysts and a phone interview after the call, NCR Chief Financial Officer John Giering said profits are weighed down by a whopping 75 percent tax rate. Giering said NCR was unlikely to bring its tax levels down to resemble industry norms of 35 to 40 percent before 1999. He said his goal was to bring the company's U.S. operations to breakeven in 1997 in terms of profitablity. NCR is already profitable in its overseas operations, which accounted for half of its $7 billion in 1996 revenues. Besides slashing the company's tax rate, the NCR executive said the company's primary goal was to see a 9 to 12 percent growth rate from core operations over the next several years. Giering said he expected NCR to reach gross profit margins in the mid-30 percent range within three years. In 1996 results released earlier Tuesday, gross margins for the year rose to 28.1 percent from 1995's 21.8 percent. Giering said profits remain small but tax liabilities are very large, hence the high effective rate. AT&T absorbed much of the potential benefit from operating loss carry-forwards when NCR was still a subsidiary, he said. On balance, AT&T relieved NCR of more than $3 billion in net losses since 1993, leaving NCR's balance sheet remarkably clean prior to its spin-off as a separate company this month. NCR said it ended 1996 with $1.2 billion in cash and debt of only $76 billion. "Right now (the tax rate) is in the 75 percent range," Giering told Reuters, "I look at this as a 1997 phenonmon." He estimated that the tax rate would come down to roughly 50 percent in 1998 on the way to the 35 to 40 percent level expected in 1999. "Clearly we need to have more income in the U.S. to turn that number around," Giering said. The company may be aided in its goal of balancing the contribution of its U.S. and international operations by trends in top-line revenue growth. Giering told analysts that the 1996 revenues for core businesses, excluding mass-market PCs and the entry level server businesses it is exiting, grew 9 percent in the Americas, but declined one percent in Europe and 3 percent in the Asia/Pacific region. NCR does not break out its revenues in dollar terms. The CFO said his primary goals was to ensure that "international operations are really paying their full share in terms of all the costs incurred on their on behalf." He said one of the anomalies NCR is working hard to reconcile is that many of its corporate functions are domiciled in the United States, which made sense as a unit of AT&T but now hurts NCR as a standalone entity at tax-time. Deep concern about NCR's financial prospects commbined with the company's insecure position in a computer industry that refuses to stand still has lead Wall Street analysts to be deeply leery of the stock since its public debut. Of the two analysts following the stock, one of them, Smith Barney's Shao Wang maintains a neutral rating. In an an unusual move on a neutral rated stock, Wang set a target price of $28 on the stock, well below its current price of $38-3/4. Nonetheless, on the strength of its ongoing turnaround, its limited fourth quarter profits and rising profit margins, NCR stock gained 3-1/8 on Tuesday. -- E. Auchard, New York newsdesk, 212-859-1736

Racal chief executive, David Elsbury, said the alliance with the U.S. consortium could yield joint savings of 100 million pounds in development costs for the British Armed Forces Bowman communications contract, due to be decided on by March 1997. The contract is crucial to Racal's future earnings and those of its existing partner, Siemens of Germany. The winner of Bowman will get an estimated two billion pounds in follow-through export orders on top of the two billion contract value. It would create 6,500 new jobs, said Elsbury. But Racal's chief warned of tough implications if the contract is lost. "To win Bowman would be the prize. To lose Bowman, God forbid, we would still have a sizeable export market, but we would have to downsize the company." He said the move by Racal and partner Siemens to link up with their U.S. rival followed news from the British government of further delays to the award process. Both sides' bids were in danger of running to 100 million apiece on research and developments costs, said Elsbury. Racal's costs to date are running at between 30 and 50 million, he said. ITT Defence said in a statement that Racal and partner Siemens, who form the Yeomans consortium, had agreed to link with its own CrossBow group on technical, production and manufacturing resources for Bowman. Racal said if they won the order, the companies would form a joint venture and each take a equity stake. Elsbury refused to comment on how the work would be split, but said "We're happy with the arrangements." The alliance news helped arrest Monday's 18 percent freefall in Racal's share price when the group issued an eleventh-hour profit warning, which triggered angry responses from shareholders, ahead of Tuesday's half-year results. Shares were up five and a half pence at 230 1/2 by 1200 GMT after closing 50 pence lower at 225 on Monday. As forecast, results for the half year to October 11 showed pre-tax profits down to 21.2 million from 30.1 million. Profits were 20 million lower than was expected this summer and were hit by a 10 million charge relating to the Data products unit. The half year payout was held at 2.10 pence and sales rose to 602 million from 502 million. Full year profits are now seen at 50 million pounds after 20 million of charges. The results fiasco was blamed by Elsbury on last minute delays in foreign government defence orders, hitting the company's revenue targets. News of the order slippage was only uncovered as late as last Friday. The defence orders were earmarked for the radio division which provides defence related equipment to foreign governments. The radio division is undergoing a strategic review which is scheduled for completion by March. Other divisions, including network services, had shown strong profit growth. The recently acquired British Rail Telecoms business was described as a "superb performer." Data Products is on the verge of a turnaround. "In the second half we should see a profit. We haven't seen that for many years," said Elsbury. ($1=.5936 Pound)

response: Ford Motor Co., following several competitors in offering "certified" used cars, said Monday its Ford and Lincoln brands are starting used vehicle warranty programme that eventually will be available nationwide. The programmes, called Ford and Lincoln Certified Pre-Owned Cars, will offer buyers extended warranties on most used Ford and Lincoln models that have undergone a rigorous inspection and reconditioning. "We're going to be very competitive in the Certified Pre-Owned market," said John McQuillen, Ford's national used vehicle sales manager. He declined to say which competitors Ford considers to be the toughest in the Certified Pre-Owned car market, but said Ford will offer "an excellent product at a fair price." The inspection and reconditioning of the used vehicles will be done by Ford and Lincoln dealers. The programmes will initially be offered in the Northeast and Midwest United States, with a national rollout expected by the end of the year. The warranties will be transferable to new buyers, and will be backed by Ford, not individual dealers. The Ford programme will offer a 12-month/12,000-mile limited powertrain warranty and a 36-month/36,000-mile limited comprehensive warranty. The Lincoln programme will offer the same powertrain coverage, but the comprehensive warranty will be good for 36 months/45,000 miles. Buyers of the certified used cars will also receive a 12-month/12,000-mile complimentary membership in Ford's roadside assistance programme. The warranty costs will vary depending on the age and condition of the used vehicle, McQuillen said. The UAW's decision to walk out at Chrysler's Canadian operations on Wednesday night gave the other Big Three U.S. automakers an opportunity to make significant progress towards national contracts covering 450,000 workers in the United States and Canada. By contrast, the bitter pattern-breaking negotiations at the local level at each of the three companies have prevented any of them from gaining the coveted "model" or "template" status for their national contracts. The UAW typically seeks outsourcing and job security improvements in local contracts, making them unusually difficult for one or more of the companies to meet, leading to a national bargaining solution. The national contracts, covering 215,000 U.S. and 235,000 Canadian workers, cover issues such as union representation, standards for new members and national health and welfare and parts sourcing costs. The local strikes and bargaining problems at each of the three companies have not been resolved, leaving the national issues unresolved as well. The UAW's national contract with Chrysler, the least profitable of the Big Three, expires on September 14. The other contracts expired on March 31. Ford and GM bargaining leaders have said they were not expecting their respective night shifts to report to work on Thursday, indicating that strikes at those companies were likely to start by then. Ford's shift workers were due to work at 9:30 a.m. EST on Thursday, while at GM, the shift change is at 11:00 a.m. EST. The UAW's Canadian Director, John Gaudet, said on Wednesday that the union gave Chrysler no warning before the strike started, leaving thousands of workers on the job until they were sent home by night shift supervisors. Chrysler said it was not prepared for the strike, saying it had given the UAW a guarantee of an extra shift on Thursday at Windsor's main truck plant, which employs 12,500 of the union's 13,000 members in Canada. "We're still trying to figure out what the heck is going on," said Chrysler spokesman John Dewar. The UAW's action at Chrysler came after a series of last-minute negotiations with the automaker aimed at delaying the strike. The union's national president, Stephen Yokich, said on Wednesday that the talks with Chrysrys were "very, very close" to an agreement. Chrysler has said it has no problem with the national contract, saying the local issues that have caused the strikes at individual plants have been resolved at General Motors and Ford. The UAW's demands for changes at individual plants have forced GM and Ford to rewrite their national contracts on the outsourcing of night shift and maintenance jobs, known as "source components," a highly costly concessions for the companies. Chrysler, the smallest of the Big Three, has said it can afford the changes demanded by the UAW, but it has not yet agreed to a pattern of local contract changes at individual plants. ------------------------------ Copyright (c) 1996, Reuters Inc. target_task: Write an article that starts with the following: The Canadian Auto Workers union's choice of Chrysler Corp as its strike target on Wednesday sets up a battle between General Motors Corp and Ford Motor Co to take the lead in bargaining with the larger United Auto Workers.

response: The Canadian Auto Workers union's choice of Chrysler Corp as its strike target on Wednesday sets up a battle between General Motors Corp and Ford Motor Co to take the lead in bargaining with the larger United Auto Workers. The UAW, which has been negotiating contract changes at all three Detroit automakers since late June, held off until the last minute before its contract with Chrysler expired at midnight (2300 GMT on Wednesday). The last-minute selection of Chrysler as the target of a national strike by 190,000 UAW members in the United States also left open the possibility of a last-minute settlement. "We're not saying there won't be a rat's night (agreement) at Chrysler," said Carl Dowell, president of UAW Local 862 at Chrysler's Livonia, Mich., truck interior parts plant. "But we've been saying for the last two weeks that Chrysler was going to be the target." The UAW's decision to hit Chrysler, the least profitable of the Detroit automakers, marked a change from the pattern of strikes in 1996 when the UAW walked shifts at GM on September 25, paralysing the world's largest automaker just two weeks after its contract expired. The UAW's president, Stephen Yokich, said on September 25 that the local strikes at GM would not be called off until he reached a national agreement with the automaker. Yokich's successor, Stuart Burgess, has not followed the same pattern, leaving open the possibility that GM's 230,000 UAW members in the United States could return to work at any time. "There's no way that Burgess is going to call off the local strikes at GM unless he has a national agreement there," said Carl Schmidt, president of UAW Local 9 at Ford's Flat Rock, Mich., car plant. "But he's not going to call the Chrysler strike off for the same members unless he has an agreement there too." Ford's 155,000 UAW members in the United States have worked under the same 1996 contract as Chrysler and GM, which expired on March 31. The UAW's contract with Chrysler, the least expensive of the Big Three automakers, has been a source of frustration for its members because it does not provide the same standard of living as the GM and Ford contracts. The UAW's demands for improvements in the pattern, including the removal of the "two-tier" wage system at Chrysler's Canadian Daytona, Fla., car door plant, are likely to result in heavy local strikes at Chrysler when the national strike ends. The local strikes at Chrysler could disrupt the company's operations in the United States and Canada, including its door, interior and battery plants, just as the national strike did in Canada in April. In Canada, the UAW's strike against Chrysler on April 30 crippled the company's operations, forcing it to halt all but a few shifts of vehicle assembly by the end of May. The strike in Canada was called off on May 26 after the UAW and Chrysler signed a national agreement covering 130,000 Canadian workers. In the United States, the UAW's walkouts have had little impact on the operations of GM and Ford, which built most of their vehicles using outside parts suppliers during the Canadian strike. The UAW's actions at Chrysler have left the leaders of GM and Ford, Jack Smith and Gerhard Schneider, waiting on the sidelines, eager to use their clout with the UAW to gain concessions from the target company. Smith and Schneider have been lobbying GM and Ford workers, respectively, for improvements in door hardware and interior parts and seats, respectively, at the target company. ----------------------------------------------------------------------- 1998 United Press International. response: The Canadian Auto Workers union's choice of Chrysler Corp as its strike target on Wednesday sets up a battle between General Motors Corp and Ford Motor Co to take the lead in bargaining with the larger United Auto Workers. The UAW's decision to strike at Chrysler's Canadian operations on September 18, 1999, over the same 21-hour shift does not mean a resolution to its contracts with GM and Ford is imminent. "It's not a hop-skip-and-a-jump from here to an agreement," said Carl Dowell, president of UAW Local 862 in Livonia, Mich., referring to the pattern of bargaining where one company settlement allows the union's national staff to fine-tune contracts at other companies. Still, the strike at Chrysler, which affected about 11,500 workers, is not expected to last long as the company and union work out details of the pattern-setting contract. That contract will cover about 170,000 UAW workers at GM, Ford and Chrysler's domestic operations. The UAW's president, Stephen Yokich, has not yet identified himself, adding to the uncertainty about the timing of a settlement. Yokich's predecessor, Bob Thomas, was identified as the bargainer in the last round of UAW talks in 1996, which were marked by bitter strikes at GM and Ford. GM and Ford were last involved in strike threats on September 12, when the UAW warned that 215,000 members at all three U.S. automakers would be ready to walk off on September 18 if no contracts were reached by then. The threat was lifted when the Canadian strike was called instead. Ford spokesman Jon Harmon said the automaker's U.S. operations were not yet involved in nightly bargaining at the company's headquarters in Dearborn, Mich. "We're not even at the table yet," he said. GM's U.S. operations were also not yet involved in the negotiations, said spokesman Charles Licari. The bargaining shifts from company to union headquarters as often as several times a day. The UAW's demands for the three contracts are expected to closely mirror those in the 1998 contract at Chrysler's Canadian Dayton Wire & Cable unit. Those demands included demands for the same "source components locally" pattern of demands that caused numerous product sourcing disputes at GM and Ford, driving off numerous outsourced parts and costing thousands of jobs. The UAW also is expected to demand signatures from top executives at each of the companies, rather than Yokich, for the contracts. Such a demand from Thomas in 1996 led to bitter disputes over the signature of GM's then-chief executive, Jack Welch, at Ford and GM's outsider, Luc Nicolles, at Chrysler. The dispute at Chrysler's Windsor, Ontario, car door plant is the first action by the UAW since the September 13 return to work of 190,000 members in the United States after a four-day threat of strikes at all three U.S. automakers. The U.S. actions were over the same issues that have been blocking settlements in Canada and the United States for a month. The issues include job security, outsouring, components sourcing, and the union's demand for a signing by Yokich or each company's chief executive. ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Copyright (c) 1999, New York Times News Service. response: The Canadian Auto Workers union's choice of Chrysler Corp as its strike target on Wednesday sets up a battle between General Motors Corp and Ford Motor Co to take the lead in bargaining with the larger United Auto Workers. The UAW's decision to walk out at Chrysler's smallest U.S. operations is not expected to delay the union's main fight over contracts covering 215,000 workers at the three biggest U.S. automakers by more than a few days. "It's not going to be a sour grapes situation where the other two say 'We want to be in and you're holding us out'," said Carl Dowell, president of UAW Local 862 in Livonia, Mich, referring to the tendency of one target company to accuse another of wanting the undesirable role just to cause trouble. By late afternoon on Wednesday, less than 24 hours after the first Canadian workers went on strike, no U.S. operations were affected. The UAW's Canadian strike over outsourcing and job security issues at Chrysler's door hinge plant in Windsor, Ontario, was expected to cost the company less than $100 million by the time it was resolved, union officials said. By contrast, the UAW's 1996 strikes at GM and Ford, which lasted 27 hours at Ford but grew into 11-day and 21/2-week walkouts respectively, cost their targets billions of dollars in lost production. The UAW's Canadian action was a signal that the U.S. strikes could begin at any time, possibly as soon as next week. The union has given no warning strikes and has often waited until the last minute to call off the Canadian action, allowing its members to return to work and apply pressure on the U.S. targets for a quick resolution there. The UAW's president, Stephen Yokich, has said he wants the U.S. contracts signed by Harry Stonecipher, the tough-nosed head of Chrysler's operations, by the time his predecessor, Vic McKenny, retires on Oct. 15. It was only at the last minute that the union told GM and Ford that it would not strike at those companies by the deadline. The UAW's pattern of bargaining often sees it threaten to strike at one company on the final day of negotiations, only to shift the target at the last minute for dramatic effect. The target then typically pays for several thousand workers to return to work within a few days, buying the rest of the bargain off for the week or more that it needs to reach a national agreement with the UAW. The shift in target does not mean that the UAW's contract at one of the other companies is free of local issues that need to be resolved. At each company, the local issues often centre on the same demands for changes to the pattern of wages and benefits that have caused heavy resistance at several US southern and eastern installations. The issues include demands for shifts to daytime work that have been rejected by workers at several night shifts, and demands for changes to the current pattern of outsourcing that have raised concerns about job security. The UAW's national demands for a signing bonus, job security and reductions in the long working night shifts to 10 hours have been less of an issue. response: Ford Motor Co., following several competitors in offering "certified" used cars, said Monday its Ford and Lincoln brands are starting used vehicle warranty programmes that eventually will be available nationwide. Under the programmes, Ford and Lincoln-Mercury dealers will put cars and trucks through special inspection and reconditioning processes and offer factory-backed warranties and three-day, money-back guarantees. "This is not just an individual, dealer programme," said Ford division spokesman Dan Bedore. "It's backed by the Ford Motor Company." The Ford Division programme will be launched in the spring following a regional rollout in the southeastern United States in mid-November, while the Lincoln programme will be introduced in major markets Dec. 9. A third programme covering Ford's Mercury brand cars and trucks will begin next summer, a Ford spokesman said. The programmes are among several now offered by major automakers, including General Motors Corp. and Toyota Motor Corp., in an effort to keep their dealers competitive in the growing market for used cars and trucks. Ample supplies of used vehicles that have come off of two-year leases have given rise to several new used-car "superstore" chains, such as Circuit City Stores Inc.'s successful CarMax unit, and a new chain called AutoNation USA, started by Blockbuster Entertainment founder H. Wayne Huizenga. Ford estimated the annual pre-owned car and truck market at 43 million units and $370 billion in revenues. Automakers are expected to sell about 15.5 million new cars and trucks in the United States this year. To qualify for the Ford Quality Certified programme, Ford brand cars and trucks must be under four years old and have been driven less than 50,000 miles. Those vehicles must pass a 100-point inspection, and following reconditioning, will receive a one-year, 12,000-mile warranty, 24-hour assistance and a three-day, 300-mile money-back guarantee. To qualify for the Lincoln Assured prgram, Lincoln luxury cars must be one-owner 1994 models or later with less than 36,000 miles and have suffered no major damage. They will undergo a 150-point inspection and will be backed by a two-year, 24,000-mile bumper-to-bumper warranty, Lincoln-Mercury said, adding that brake pads will be replaced on all Lincoln cars with more than 25,000 miles.

GM said the costs associated with the U.S. and Canadian strikes came to $700 million, or 91 cents a share. The Canadian Auto Workers was on strike for three weeks in October over contract negotiations with the automaker, causing factory shutdowns in the United States. GM was still reeling from the Canadian walkout when UAW members staged local strikes at a metal stamping plant in Indianapolis and a truck plant in Janesville, Wis., which forced GM to idle more workers. Earlier Thursday, Hughes announced a management shakeup for Kokomo, Ind.-based Delco, naming Michael Burns as general manager, replacing the retiring Gary Dickinson. Burns was previously in charge of GM's Delphi Thermal Systems unit which makes vehicle radiators and climate control systems.

In a hearing before the Senate Banking Committee, senators questioned SEC commissioners David Verrecchia and Paul Roye, both of whom helped draft the final version of the rule issued last week by the commission. The rule requires companies to disclose in their filings with the SEC how they use derivatives, financial instruments with a value based on an underlying asset or index, such as a stock, commodity or currency. Senators raised objections on several fronts, including the cost of complying with the rule, the breadth of the disclosures required and the potential impact on innovation. "I think this is a very, very troubling regulation," Sen. William Cohen, R-Maine, said. "I think it imposes a significant burden on American business." Senators also expressed concern that the rule might discourage the use of derivatives to manage risk. "I'm afraid this disclosure requirement may backfire and cause some companies to shy away from using derivatives to hedge risks," Sen. Charles Schumer, D-N.Y., said. Commissioners Verrecchia and Roye defended the rule, saying it would improve the quality of information available to investors. "The disclosures required by the rule are designed to provide investors with useful information about a company's use of derivatives," Verrecchia said. "We believe the rule strikes an appropriate balance between the need for disclosure and the potential burden on companies." The SEC issued the rule to implement a provision of the Financial Institutions Regulatory and Examination Privacy Act, which Congress passed in 1996. The act requires all publicly traded companies to disclose their use of derivatives. The commission received more than 3,000 comments on the proposed rule, which was issued in December 1997. The final rule is similar to the proposed version, but commissioners made some changes to ease concerns raised in the comments. For example, the final rule allows companies to omit individual derivative transactions if the aggregate value of the transactions is insignificant. The proposed rule would have required companies to disclose all transactions. Commissioners also broadened the types of derivatives that could be excluded from the disclosure requirement if the company used them only for hedging. Under the final rule, a company can exclude such derivatives if they represent less than 10 percent of the total value of all derivatives the company uses. Under the proposed rule, the threshold was 5 percent. The commissioners also added a provision allowing companies to omit disclosure of derivatives used solely for trading if the company's total revenue from such activities does not exceed 25 percent of its total revenue. The proposed rule did not include such a provision. The rule takes effect on Oct. 1, but companies will not have to comply until they file their next quarterly report with the SEC. "We were disappointed that the Fed did not take this opportunity to outline specific initiatives to address the lack of diversity at the highest levels of the central bank," they said in a statement. response:
Two members of Congress criticised the Federal Reserve Thursday for what they called its "woefully inadequate" record of hiring and promoting women and minorities. Representatives Barbara Lee, Democrat of California, and Maxine Waters, Democrat of California and a member of the House Financial Services Committee, wrote in a letter to Fed chairman Alan Greenspan that the central bank's workforce "lags far behind the diversity of the American workforce" in the categories of race, ethnicity, gender and disability. The lawmakers said that only 12 percent of the Fed's 2,800 employees are minorities, and that no African Americans or Hispanics hold senior policy-making positions. Among women, only 29 percent of the employees are in professional or managerial jobs, the letter said. Lee and Waters also criticised the Fed for not collecting data on employees' sexual orientation or age. The lawmakers asked Greenspan to set diversity goals for the central bank and to report back to Congress on the progress being made towards meeting those goals. The Fed's diversity record is "of great concern to us, as it should be to all Americans," the letter said. "A diverse workforce brings with it a broader range of ideas, experiences and perspectives. The Fed's failure to foster such an environment is not only bad policy, it is bad business." The Fed responded that it was making efforts to improve its diversity record. "We believe that the Fed is making progress in this area," Fed spokeswoman Catherine Tymkiw said. "We have a number of initiatives under way to increase the diversity of the workforce." Tymkiw said the central bank was working with universities to attract a more diverse pool of applicants for its jobs. She said the Fed was also setting up a task force to review its hiring and promotion policies.  (c) Reuters 2001. All rights reserved. In the United States, the cost of congestion to trucking alone is estimated at $25 billion a year. The Leesburg Pike is just one example of the problem. Across the country, highways and roads are clogged with trucks trying to move goods. As container ships continue to grow in size, the ports and infrastructure to handle them have not kept pace, leading to delays and backups. The International Trade Administration reported that U.S. imports of goods by sea grew 3.5% in 2020, despite the overall economic contraction caused by the pandemic. The global supply chain is snarled, and the result is higher prices for consumers and strained inventories for retailers and manufacturers. Here's a look at what's causing the backup and where the solutions might lie. The root of the problem is the size of container ships. The largest ships can carry 20,000 or more containers, up from 1,000 or so a few decades ago. The increased capacity is a response to market demand. Retailers and manufacturers want to get their goods to market as quickly and cheaply as possible. The bigger ships reduce the number of trips needed to transport the same volume of goods. But the ships are too big for many ports. The Panama Canal, for example, did not allow ships larger than about 13,000 containers to pass through until 2016. The expansion of the canal has helped, but the largest ships still cannot make it through the Suez Canal, which is a key shipping route between Europe and Asia. As a result, ports around the world are racing to deepen their channels and expand their terminals to accommodate the larger ships. The Port of Virginia, for example, is investing $1 billion to deepen its harbor and expand its terminals. But the work is expensive and time-consuming. The Port of Los Angeles/Long Beach, the busiest container port in the world, has been working to expand since the late 1990s and still isn't finished. The backup at the ports is causing ships to wait at anchor for days or even weeks to be unloaded. That's leading to delays in getting goods to market and to consumers. The situation is particularly acute for perishable goods, such as fruits and vegetables. The delay can mean the difference between a good harvest and a ruined one. The backup is also causing headaches for truckers and railroads trying to move the goods from the ports to warehouses and distribution centers. The lack of available containers is another problem. Container lines own most of the containers and rent them out to shippers. The lines have been slow to add new containers to the fleet because the cost of building a new one is about $3,000, while they can be rented for $1,000 or more a month. The shortage of containers is causing some shippers to buy their own. That's what Home Depot did when it bought 3,500 containers last year. The home improvement retailer plans to use them to move goods directly from the factories to its stores, bypassing the ports altogether. The backup at the ports is also causing higher shipping costs. The container lines are able to charge more because they have the market power. The situation is likely to get worse before it gets better. The global economy is recovering from the pandemic and demand for goods is growing. The container lines are ordering even larger ships. Maersk, the world's largest container line, has ordered 11 ships that can carry 23,000 containers each. The ships are scheduled for delivery starting in 2023. The solutions are not easy or cheap. The ports need to deepen their channels and expand their terminals. The governments and industries along shipping routes need to build new locks, such as a larger one at the Panama Canal, or find alternative routes, such as the northern one through Russia. The container lines need to build more containers and the shippers need to buy their own. The consumers may have to pay higher prices for some goods until the supply chain catches up. In the meantime, commuters on the Leesburg Pike will continue to be reminded of the global logistics jam every time they sit in traffic.

The Leesburg Pike, also known as Route 7, is a major artery for commerce in the Washington, D.C., area. Every day, trucks laden with everything from office supplies to computers make their way along the route, which is lined with warehouses, distribution centers and corporate offices. The traffic is heaviest during the morning and evening rush hours, when thousands of workers head to and from their jobs. But the real traffic jam is taking place at the ports and borders where these goods are shipped and received. "The real bottleneck is not here on Route 7," said Tom Cutter, president of the Northern Virginia Transportation Alliance. "It's at the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach, and at the borders of Mexico and Canada." Exports from the United States and imports from around the world move through these ports at an astonishing rate. More than 13,000 containers, each holding the equivalent of a standard 20-foot truckload, are handled at the ports each day. But getting those containers to their final destinations can be a slow process. On average, it takes 10 days to move a container from the ports to a distributor in the United States. That's up from six days just a few years ago. The delay costs businesses billions of dollars each year in increased inventory holding costs and lost sales. To ease the congestion, some companies are turning to new transportation technologies, such as intermodal rail and electronic data interchange. Intermodal rail allows containers to be moved from ship to rail to truck without being unloaded. EDI, on the other hand, allows the electronic exchange of shipping information between companies, reducing the time spent waiting for paperwork to be processed. But these solutions don't come cheap. Intermodal rail costs about $1,000 to move a container from coast to coast, compared to $3,000 by truck. And implementing EDI requires computer systems that can cost tens of thousands of dollars. "There's no question that these new technologies will help," Cutter said. "But they're not going to solve the problem overnight. We're going to have to invest in infrastructure, too." That means building more ports, expanding highways and improving border crossings. But with budgets already stretched thin, getting governments to invest in such projects may be difficult. "We've got to make sure our elected officials understand that this is not just a nice-to-have issue, it's a have-to-have issue," Cutter said. "Without a transportation system that works, our economy doesn't work." 

In the end, the solution to the transportation jam may be as simple as getting everyone moving in the same direction. "We need to focus on reducing the number of steps it takes to move a product from the port to the customer," said John Langley, vice president of global logistics for DHL Worldwide Express. "That means reducing customs delays, reducing trucking delays, reducing rail delays. It means streamlining the whole process." And while that may not be as easy as turning around a car stuck in traffic and going the other way, it just might get things moving in the right direction.

response: Britain's commercial property market may be improving but it has not yet got a clean bill of health, a senior Bank of England official said on Wednesday. "The commercial property market is showing some signs of improvement but it's not out of the woods yet," Brian Pepperell, the Bank's executive director for financial stability, told an audience at the Investment Property Forum in London. He said the recovery was not unexpected given the long business cycle but it was not as strong as might have been expected in the light of a strong economy. Pepperell warned that the market could be hit by a number of factors including the increasing amount of office space being developed, the impact of the Internet on retailing and the fact that rents are only just keeping pace with inflation. "The fact that real rents are only just keeping pace with inflation is a cause for concern," he said. He also highlighted the problem of high levels of debt in the commercial property sector and the fact that much of it was coming due in the next few years. "A lot of people are going to have to refinance and the question is at what price," he said. But Pepperell said he was encouraged by the fact that vacancy rates were falling and that take-up of space was strong in the industrial sector. He also noted that foreign investment had returned to the market and that yields were starting to harden. "But yields are still high in real terms and that's a concern," he added. Pepperell said the recovery in the commercial property market was not being reflected in the residential sector where prices continued to rise strongly. He warned that this could lead to problems in the future. "The housing market is still going up and up and up and that's a concern," he said. Pepperell also touched on the issue of the Bank's role in the event of a major problem in the financial sector, saying it would have to decide whether to step in and take corrective action. "We would have to decide whether we have an interest and if we do what is the most appropriate way to deal with the problem," he said. But he stressed that the Bank would not be in the business of rescuing individual companies. "We are not going to be in the business of bailing out companies," he added. response: London will defend its share of foreign exchange trading once a single European currency comes into being, according new Lord Mayor of London Judith Mayhew said on Thursday. "I am going to be out there batting for the Square Mile. I don't think we are going to lose a great deal of our business. I think we are going to have to work very hard to keep it, but I am confident we will," Mayhew, who took over the ceremonial role from David Walker, told Reuters in an interview. Asked if she would have to defend London's position as a leading global financial centre in the context of a single European currency, Mayhew replied: "Yes, I will have to defend our share of foreign exchange trading. I think we will have to work very hard to keep that. "But I am optimistic. I think we are going to be in a position to attract a lot of the euro business. I don't think we are going to lose a great deal," she said. Mayhew, who was the first woman to be appointed to the role, acknowledged that the financial industry would have to adapt to the challenges posed by the single currency. "The industry is going to have to change. It is going to have to become much more European. It is going to have to learn to operate in a much more integrated way," she said. Mayhew, who was a deputy governor of the Bank of England from 1988 to 1992 and is the first Lord Mayor to have held a senior job at the central bank, said she would use her position to promote Britain and the City of London around the world. "I am going to be an ambassador for this country. I am going to be out there banging the drum for Britain," she said. Mayhew, who will represent the City of London on the world stage for the next year, said she would also be using her position to promote charitable causes and to encourage greater participation by women in the financial industry and in business in general. "I am going to be using this position to try and encourage more women into business and into the financial services industry," she said. Mayhew, who was born in 1944 and educated at the University of Birmingham, said she would be living in the Lord Mayor's official residence, the Mansion House, with her husband. She said she would be the working Lord Mayor, with her husband taking on the role of consort at formal events. ------------------------------------------------------------------- This article is a part of Reuters News, which is among the leading global providers of business news and financial information. response: Markets across Eastern Europe remained mired in an autumn slump this week, with analysts seeing little on the horizon to break the bearish trend. The Prague Stock Exchange's PX50 index of leading shares dipped 0.39 percent after two straight sessions of gains, while the Budapest BUX-40 index in Hungary eased 0.18 percent after falling sharply on Monday. "There's no real reason for the market to move up. We're still waiting for some good news," said one local analyst, adding that foreign investors were continuing to take their money out of the region. In neighbouring Slovakia, the Slovak Blue Chip Index (SBI) fell 1.28 percent after a brief rally on Monday following the election of a centre-right coalition government. The Warsaw Stock Exchange's WIG20 index in Poland bucked the trend, rising 0.44 percent after a 2.22 percent fall on Monday, but local analysts said the gain was due to a single share -- telecoms giant Polska Telefonia Cyfrowa (PTC) -- which rose 8.63 percent after a court ruling on Monday allowed it to merge with rival Plus. Most other shares on the Warsaw market fell, and overall turnover was light at 1.14 billion zlotys ($305.7 million). Czech markets have been particularly hard hit in recent weeks, with the PX50 index falling 12.63 percent since October 1, when it hit an all-time high of 533.28 points. Analysts blame the weakness on a slowing Czech economy, a political crisis in neighbouring Slovakia, and jitters ahead of parliamentary elections due in the Czech Republic on November 25-26. They also say that foreign investors -- who have bought up around 70 percent of the traded volume on the Prague market in recent months -- have been spooked by rising Czech interest rates, which hit a record 7.50 percent this month. "The market is being driven by foreigners, and they are selling," said one local broker. "They don't like the economic situation, they don't like the political situation, and they don't like the high interest rates." In Hungary, the market has been hit by a series of scandals involving local privatisation, and by uncertainty over economic reforms following the election of a centre-left coalition government in May. The BUX-40 index has fallen 13.21 percent since it hit a post-election high of 4895.95 points on June 23. Analysts say the market is likely to remain weak until the government unveils a new economic programme in the autumn. -- Prague Newsroom, 42-2-2423-0000 01-242-207-207 (editorial) 01-242-207-202 (news desk) 01-242-207-208 (fax)

The index is down more than 50 percent since the beginning of the year, and the central bank's latest interest rate hike failed to boost investor confidence. response: The Prague Stock Exchange continued to gain ground on Thursday, but analysts said they are not convinced the beleaguered bourse's fortunes have turned around, attributing the rise to thin domestic buying. The Czech benchmark PX50 index rose 1.02 percent, or 13.25 points, to 1304.75 after two sessions of heavy losses. But local analysts said they saw little substance in the rise, with foreign investors continuing to shun the market and domestic buying thin. "I'd be very cautious about reading too much into this rise," said one local analyst, who asked not to be named. "It looks to me like we're seeing mostly small, institutional investors buying, not the big players." The local market has been hit hard by recent losses on the world's major bourses, with the PX50 shedding 5.4 percent on Wednesday following a 3.6 percent fall on Tuesday. The Czech bourse has been particularly hard hit by the withdrawal of foreign funds following the central bank's decision in January to raise interest rates to curb inflation. The Czech Republic's inflation rate rose to 5.3 percent in February, the highest since the central bank began publishing monthly figures in 1995. Prague's bourse has also been hit by the uncertainty surrounding the government's efforts to pass a controversial privatisation law, which would force foreign investors to sell their stakes in Czech companies to local partners if they do not buy out minority shareholders. response: Chinese dissident Liu Xiaobo has filed a lawsuit against Beijing authorities for sending him to a labour camp without trial, his wife said on Tuesday. Liu, a former Beijing university professor and one of China's most prominent dissidents, was sent to a labour camp in Dalian in northeastern Liaoning province in December 1995 for writing and distributing a petition calling for democratic reforms. "I have already sent the lawsuit to the Dalian labour bureau," Liu's wife, Liu Xia, said by telephone from her home in Beijing. She said she had handed the lawsuit to a friend who was going to Dalian on Monday to deliver it to the labour bureau. The lawsuit, which Liu wrote himself, accuses Beijing authorities of violating the law by sending him to the labour camp without a trial, Liu Xia said. She said she hoped the lawsuit would bring attention to Liu's case and help him regain his freedom. "I hope this lawsuit will attract the attention of the media and the public," Liu Xia said. She said she had no information on whether Beijing authorities would allow Liu to hire a lawyer to represent him in court. China's state-controlled courts are widely seen as biased against dissidents and rarely rule in their favour. Liu, 43, is one of about 100 dissidents who have been targeted in a crackdown by Beijing against intellectuals and activists calling for more democracy and an end to official corruption. He was one of the organisers of the Tiananmen Square demonstrations in Beijing in 1989 that were crushed by the army with tanks and machine guns, killing hundreds, possibly thousands, of people. Liu was sentenced to 11 years in prison in January 1990 for his role in the demonstrations. He was released on medical parole in July 1993 because of liver and kidney problems. He was allowed to live under virtual house arrest in Beijing after his release. In December 1995, Beijing authorities sent him to the labour camp for writing and distributing the petition calling for democratic reforms. The Chicago-based finance company also said it would default on $220 million of debt because it could not meet interest payments. "The company has determined that it lacks sufficient resources to pay the $17 million of commercial debt that is due today and that it intends to default on the $220 million of its debt," Mercury said in a statement. The company's stock was suspended from trading Friday after falling 86 cents, or 86 percent, to 1 cent on the Nasdaq stock market. "The company's inability to pay the commercial debt is also causing the company's other creditors and the company's off-balance sheet financing arrangers to take actions to accelerate the company's other debt obligations for immediate payment," Mercury said. The company also said its offices were closed to visitors and that it was taking steps to reorganize under federal bankruptcy laws. "The company's board of directors is taking steps to institute proceedings under the United States Bankruptcy Code," Mercury said. A message left for the company's investor relations department was not immediately returned. Mercury Finance provides financing for the sale of automobiles and other consumer goods, often to customers with poor credit histories. The company reported $24.6 million in losses for the first three months of 1997, wider than the $10.8 million loss reported in the same period a year ago. The company also said at the time that it was having trouble selling some of the financing it had already recorded as assets on its books. Analysts said the company's problems were likely due to a tightening of credit in the finance industry and a slowdown in the sales of the automobiles and other goods that Mercury finances. "It's a credit crunch," said Thomas Burns, an analyst at Sanders Brandon & Cohodes Inc. "The financing of subprime [credit] is getting tougher." The company said it was cooperating with an inquiry by the Securities and Exchange Commission and that it expected to file a report detailing the accounting issues with the NASDAQ market. The collapse of the buyout deal came a day after shareholders of the consumer finance business, First Financial Holdings Corp., were scheduled to vote on the proposed acquisition of their company by Mercury. "First Financial Holdings Corp. is a financially sound company with a strong balance sheet and a proven business model," the statement said. Hitchcock said he was not surprised by the news, noting that Mercury had reported earnings below analysts' expectations in each of the last three quarters. "This is something that's been brewing," he said. But he said he was not yet ready to write off the stock. "I'm not ready to throw the baby out with the bath water," he said. The unexpected developments at Dallas-based Mercury forced Minneapolis-based Household International Inc. to scrap their $1.5 billion merger agreement, which was announced just 11 days ago. "Based on information that has come to Household's attention since the signing of the merger agreement, Household is not able to continue to satisfy the continuing conditions to the completion of the merger," Household said in a statement. Those conditions include the approval of Household's stockholders and the satisfaction of federal antitrust laws. Mercury said it is investigating the fake entries, which occurred during the first three quarters of 1996. The entries added about $30 million to Mercury's reported earnings, the company said. Mercury's stock fell 1-1/4 to 3-5/16 Thursday on the NASDAQ, while Household's stock fell 1-1/8 to 53-1/8. "This is obviously a serious matter, but until the investigation is completed, it's impossible to say what the implications are," said John Dunn, an analyst at Gerard Klauer Mattison & Co. Dunn said he did not expect the breakdown of the merger to have any effect on Household, which is the parent company of the credit card giant, Visa. "This is just a matter for Mercury," he said. Mercury said its investigation is being conducted with the help of its outside auditor, Arthur Andersen & Co. "Mercury Finance is cooperating with the investigation and is committed to taking all necessary actions to correct the situation," the company said in a statement. Mercury Finance is the largest originator of subprime auto loans in the United States, making loans to buyers who do not qualify for prime financing. The company sells the loans to investors and keeps the financing fees. Household is the largest provider of credit cards and other consumer credit in the United States and Europe. The companies said in their Oct. 21 statement announcing the merger that the deal was expected to be completed in the first quarter of 1997. The statement also said that Mercury Finance would become a subsidiary of Household and that Mercury Finance's common stock would be cancelled or exchanged for Household stock. But in Thursday's statement, Household said that the merger agreement had been terminated and that Mercury Finance remained an independent company. "There is no change in the ownership of Mercury Finance's common stock," Household said. Dunn said it was unclear whether the termination of the merger agreement would give other suitors an opportunity to make a bid for Mercury Finance. "I don't think there's any other company out there waiting in the wings," he said. But he noted that other finance companies, such as General Finance Corp. and First Chicago NBD Corp., have made bids for other finance companies in the past year. "I think there's always a possibility," he said. Mercury Finance said it would release its third quarter earnings on Nov. 7. response: Australia's largest home mortgage lender, the Commonwealth Bank of Australia (CBA), announced a surprisingly strong 11 percent surge in first half 1996/97 profits on Wednesday, despite erosion of its interest margins. The profit rise to A$1.11 billion (US$972 million) was well above market expectations of a seven to 10 percent increase. "It's a very solid result," CBA Chief Executive Ralph Norfolk told a news conference. "We're very pleased with it," he said, adding that the bank's core businesses were performing well and that there was no need for it to raise capital at the moment. Norfolk said that while net interest margins had fallen to 1.63 percent from 1.67 percent in the first half, this was largely due to the fall in short term interest rates and that overall earnings from lending were still strong. "But the bottom line is that we're still making a lot of money out of lending," he said. "The loan book is growing at about 12 percent and the margin on that is still quite healthy," he said. "Overall we're quite happy with where we are," he said. "We're still in the market to sell 20 percent of Colonial," Norfolk said. "We're still talking to people and we'll do it when we get a reasonable price," he said. response:
Ford Motor Co., following several competitors in offering "certified" used cars, said Monday its Ford and Lincoln brands are starting used vehicle warranty programme that eventually will be available nationwide. The programs, which begin this month in the Midwest and expand to other regions later this year, offer buyers of used Ford and Lincoln cars up to 12 months of coverage against most mechanical failures, Ford said. The coverage, which can be transferred to subsequent owners, costs $200 to $350, depending on the car's model and age. "We're trying to take the uncertainty out of buying a used car," said John McFarlane, Ford's national used vehicle manager. "We want to give people the same confidence they have when they buy a new car." Ford's program, which is similar to those offered by General Motors Corp. and Chrysler Corp., requires that all used cars sold under the Ford and Lincoln certifications undergo a 134-point inspection. Any parts that do not meet Ford specifications are either replaced or refinished. The inspections are performed by Ford and Lincoln dealers. "This is a very stringent inspection," McFarlane said. "We're looking for cars that are in excellent condition." Under the programme, cars that fail the inspection cannot be sold as certified used cars, but they still can be sold on the open market. Ford said it plans to provide customers with a history of each used car, including details of previous owners, accident damage and maintenance records. The automaker also is considering an inspection and certification programme for its commercial vehicles, such as delivery trucks and school buses, McFarlane said. The certification programmes are part of Ford's efforts to expand its used car operations and compete more effectively with GM and Chrysler, which have been offering certified used cars for several years. "We've been late to the party," McFarlane said. "But we're not late any more." Ford has been expanding its used car operations in other ways, including the opening of a used car call centre and the hiring of used car sales trainers. The automaker also is considering allowing its dealers to advertise used cars on the Internet, McFarlane said. "We're trying to make our used car operations more professional and more efficient," he said. 

Despite the expansion of its used car operations, Ford does not plan to discontinue the sale of most of its cars through independent used car dealers, McFarlane said. "We're not going to cut off the independent used car dealers," he said. "We're going to sell the majority of our used cars through them." 

The certification programmes come as Ford is under intense pressure to improve its financial performance. The automaker has been plagued by high discounts on its cars, which have eroded its profit margins. In addition, Ford's truck and sport utility vehicle lines, which have been its most profitable products, also have been hit by increased competition and a slowing market. 

Ford's stock was up 1/4 to 41 1/2 on the New York Stock Exchange.

There are several steps you can take to reduce food waste at home: 

1. Plan your meals: Make a weekly meal plan based on what ingredients you have on hand. This will help you use the food you buy and prevent it from going bad.

2. Shop smart: Make a list before you go shopping and stick to it. Avoid buying large quantities of perishable items unless you know you'll use them before they go bad.

3. Store food properly: Make sure you're storing your food correctly to maximize its shelf life. For example, keep fruits and vegetables in the crisper drawer and store grains and pastas in airtight containers.

4. Use your freezer: Freeze leftovers or ingredients you won't use right away. This is a great way to extend the life of your food and reduce waste.

5. Get creative in the kitchen: Use your imagination to find new ways to use ingredients before they go bad. For example, wilted greens can be used to make smoothies, and stale bread can be turned into croutons.

6. Compost: If you have a garden or access to a community compost program, consider composting your food scraps instead of throwing them away. This is a great way to reduce waste and enrich the soil.

7. Donate: If you have excess food that you won't be able to use before it goes bad, consider donating it to a local food bank or shelter. This is a great way to help those in need and reduce waste at the same time.

Pictures. Stories. Credit Card numbers. Everything is out there for the world to see. Most people don’t even enable security features; even more don’t know security features exist. We have things like Facebook.com, and Myspace.com. These were originally made as networking sites. Myspace.com came first. It allowed people to make profiles, send messages, and post bulletins. You aren’t supposed to be able to have a Myspace.com account until you are fifteen, however, no one checks and so it easy for children to lie and retain an account. What was originally a networking web site, has now become a free for all of teenagers and college students playing around on the Internet, showing off their mischief. Let’s move on to Facebook. Originally a networking site meant for college students. You had to have a valid college email address to have a profile. Rather recently it was opened to the public. Students have pictures of them drinking underage, engaging in numerous illicit and illegal activities. They don’t seem to realize that things on the Internet are open to everyone. Once something is anywhere on the Internet it is public domain. The Internet is a public domain. You put it out there someone is going to see it. Your RA, your principal, your teachers, or even your parents. Don’t be shocked if you get a phone call about a picture, which was shown, to your parents of you “totally wasted”. In reference to the situation in the prompt, no, it’s not an invasion of privacy. First of all, to see bulletin’s on Myspace.com you have to be that person’s MySpace “friend”. It does not seem like the teachers were trolling the MySpace boards just trying to find problems. It seems that this was brought to their attention by another student. How can that be an invasion of privacy? The job of the supervisors at the school was to protect the majority of the students, not only teach them. They had to act even though this may have just been a joke by this student. I think this example should show teens as well as children and adults that when you say something, especially on the Internet, it can come back to haunt you. You could be joking, you could be serious, perhaps you just weren’t thinking but these things can come back to haunt you. This is a big issue in colleges right now, due to Facebook. Students post pictures of them at parties, or drinking with their friends. They forget that their RA, and their dean , and their teachers ,and even their parents could easily have a facebook account and be viewing these pictures. Some colleges are even using facebook pictures as “evidence” in the judicial process. There’s a fine line, but people need to realize that once you put something on the internet, it’s no longer private.

response: What really is “gay marriage”? It is a socially, governmentally, and religiously recognized marriage in which two people of the same sex live together as a family. Many supportive of same-sex marriage often use the term "equal marriage" to stress that they seek equality as opposed to special rights. Opponents argue that equating same-sex and opposite-sex marriage changes the meaning of marriage and its traditions. I feel that the suggestion of reserving the word "marriage" for religious contexts, and in civil and legal contexts using a uniform concept of civil unions is the best answer. Does our declaration not say all men are created equal? So, why should same sex couples be denied the same rights as heterosexual couples? I feel that civil unions between same sex couples should have identical legal status to a marriage, and partners gain all the same benefits and associated legal rights; ranging from tax exemptions and joint property rights, to next of kin status, and shared parenting responsibilities. Those who advocate that marriage should be defined exclusively as the union of one man and one woman argue that heterosexual unions provide the procreative foundation of the family unit that is the chief social building block of civilization. My issue with this argument is that then we should not allow couples that cannot have children to be married either. Also, those who do not plan to have children should also not be allowed to be married. The procreation argument cannot reasonably be used against same-sex marriage, particularly since technological advances allow gay couples to have their own related biological children. Supporters also argue that making it available to more people would strengthen the institution of marriage, and furthermore that same-sex marriage would encourage gays and lesbians to settle down with one partner and raise families. Others argue that marriage no longer retains a procreative function of the government since many governments offer child tax credits and assistance regardless of marital status. The example in our government of calling marriage an institution between a man and a woman infuriates me. It is just a bit more proof of the fact that the separation between church and state no longer exists. The fact that our president called for an amendment banning even a civil union between same sex couples is appalling. The president is the last person who should be allowing his religious opinions to cloud his judgment. It is understandable that gay marriage inspires its own set of passions, with opponents decrying it as a step that will undermine the very fabric of society while supporters posit it as an inevitable next stage in step-by-step acceptance of homosexuality by mainstream America. But why, is that wrong? Should we not accept our fellow man in all his many shapes and sizes. If religiosity is the main contender against gay marriage, is it not true that most religions advocate acceptance and the matter of turning the other cheek. My belief is that homosexual couples are no different from heterosexual couples and should be treated as such.

Since then, marriage has evolved from a simple partnership between two people and their gods to a complex legal and social contract between two individuals. Now, as the new millennia dawns, marriage is once again at a crossroads. The question of whether to admit homosexuals into the hallowed institution has divided our great nation as no other moral issue has in decades. As a man of reason, I cannot simply dismiss one side or the other as wrong without careful consideration.

The arguments against homosexual marriage are deeply rooted in tradition and religious doctrine. Marriage, we are told, is a sacred bond between a man and a woman. It is through this union that children are born and the cycle of life continues. Homosexual marriage, it is argued, cannot produce children and therefore is not a legitimate form of marriage. This is where the lines of reason become blurred. Many heterosexual marriages do not produce children. Many do not even last very long. Should these marriages then be considered any less valid than one which may produce offspring? The answer, of course, is no. Marriage is about much more than just procreation. It is about companionship, commitment, and love.

The other side of this argument, the pro-gay marriage faction, is just as passionate in its beliefs. Homosexuals, it is argued, should have the same rights and privileges as any other American. They should be able to marry the person they love, just as any heterosexual man or woman can. This is where the lines of morality become blurred. The bible, which many argue is the foundation of western civilization, teaches us that it is a sin to lie, to steal, and to covet that which belongs to another man. It also teaches us that it is a sin for a man to lie with another man. This is where the lines of reason and morality must be separated. The bible was written over 2,000 years ago. Its teachings were meant for a much simpler time, a time when life expectancy was much lower and knowledge was much more limited. To continue to use the bible as a moral guide in the 21st century is to be just as ignorant as those ancient peoples were.

So, do I believe either side is right or wrong? I cannot answer that question with the same level of certainty that I would like to. I do believe, however, that the side which advocates change, that side which would admit homosexuals into the institution of marriage, is the side which is closer to being right. Marriage, as I have stated before, is about much more than just procreation. It is about companionship, commitment, and love. There is no reason why that love should be limited to those of opposite sexes. In a perfect world, all men would be created equal. In a perfect world, all men would be allowed to marry the woman they love. In a perfect world, all men would be allowed to marry the man he loves. 

Unfortunately, we do not live in a perfect world. We live in a world where ignorance and fear still run rampant. We must continue to educate ourselves and others about the homosexual lifestyle.
